articles.title: Memory Chip Crunch and Semiconductor Trade (AMD-Samsung, Samsung Q3, Micron) - Gotrade
articles.summary: Memory Chip Crunch and Semiconductor Trade (AMD-Samsung, Samsung Q3, Micron)  Gotrade
articles.full_text:
Gotrade News - Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) CEO Lisa Su met Samsung Electronics chip head Jun Young-hyun in Seoul on Wednesday to deepen high-bandwidth memory ties, as a global memory shortage persists.
Samsung reports preliminary third-quarter results on Thursday, with analysts expecting operating profit of about 106 trillion won.
The talks land in the same week that memory makers are cashing in on tight supply. Micron Technology (MU) has already said conditions will get "much tighter" through 2028, a message that followed its record fiscal fourth quarter, as reported by The Korea Herald.
AMD and MU Market Data
| Ticker | Close | Daily change | Market cap | 52-week range | 
|---|---|---|---|---|
| AMD | $649.42 | +2.80% | $1.06 trillion | $188.22 to $658.52 | 
| MU | $1,045.56 | -1.73% | $1.18 trillion | $179.61 to $1,255.00 | 
Regular-session close on October 6, 2026, New York time. Prices and changes: Yahoo Finance, cross-checked against Nasdaq's official close. Market cap: Nasdaq, as of October 7, 2026.
Why Is AMD CEO Lisa Su Meeting Samsung?
Su is meeting Samsung to secure and expand AI memory cooperation, centered on high-bandwidth memory (HBM). According to SBS, Su met Jun, Vice Chairman and Head of Samsung's Device Solutions Division, at Samsung's Seocho building in Seoul, and also held her first South Korea meeting with SK Hynix President and CEO Kwak Noh-jung.
Per SBS, Samsung currently supplies HBM3E and HBM4 for AMD's AI accelerators and has been designated the primary HBM4 supplier for AMD's next-generation Instinct MI455X accelerator.
SBS added that a potential foundry partnership could also be on the table. The visit follows Su's March 2026 trip, when she toured Samsung's Pyeongtaek facility and met Chairman Lee Jae-yong.
Advanced Micro Devices (AMD): Locking In HBM4 Supply
For AMD, memory access is a direct input into its AI accelerator roadmap. SBS reported that the discussions focused on strengthening collaboration in AI semiconductors, particularly HBM, with Su also attending an AI semiconductor roundtable in Seoul during the trip.
The shortage is not limited to AI chips. According to The Korea Herald, tight supply now extends beyond HBM into conventional server, PC and mobile memory, contributing to broader price increases across the sector.
Micron Technology (MU): Shortage Seen Lasting Through 2028
Micron's latest results give the clearest read on the crunch. As reported by The Korea Herald, Micron posted record fiscal fourth-quarter revenue of $54.23 billion, nearly five times the $11.32 billion a year earlier, and said more than 75% of its planned fiscal 2027 output is already committed to customers.
Per the same report, Micron now has 26 strategic customer agreements, up from 16 in June, with customer financial commitments of $32 billion.
CEO Sanjay Mehrotra said memory and storage conditions would be "much tighter" in fiscal 2027 and 2028 than in 2026.
What Does Wall Street Expect From Samsung's Q3 Results?
Analysts expect a record quarter. According to Investing.com, the LSEG SmartEstimate from 21 analysts puts Samsung's third-quarter operating profit at 106.1 trillion won ($79.1 billion), roughly nine times the 12.17 trillion won reported a year earlier and a fourth consecutive record.
The Korea Herald cited a higher consensus of 110.3 trillion won, which would be Samsung's first quarterly operating profit above 100 trillion won.
| Samsung Q3 2026 estimate (preliminary results due Oct 8) | Figure | Source | 
|---|---|---|
| Operating profit, LSEG SmartEstimate | 106.1 trillion won | Investing.com | 
| Operating profit, consensus | 110.3 trillion won | The Korea Herald | 
| Revenue, consensus | 204.8 trillion won | Investing.com | 
| Operating profit, Q3 2025 | 12.17 trillion won | Investing.com | 
Investing.com also noted that Samsung shares had fallen for two straight sessions ahead of the release and that operating profit estimates have been cut 7.7% since late August.
The preliminary release will carry only headline sales and operating profit, with segment detail due with the full report on October 29.
Are Memory Prices Peaking?
That is the main question beyond the headline numbers. Per Investing.com, the pace of chip price increases slowed in the third quarter, and Bernstein expects conventional memory prices to rise by mid-teens to 20% quarter over quarter in Q3, with single-digit increases projected for Q4.
Investing.com added that analysts see the durability of AI capital spending as the largest risk, while long-term supply agreements guarantee volume but cap price gains.
According to The Korea Herald, Samsung has signed such agreements with five major data-center customers, and SK Hynix has completed negotiations with about 10 customers on contracts generally running around five years.

articles.title: AMD’s Lisa Su Visits South Korea, Reportedly Discusses AI Collaboration With Samsung, SK Hynix - Asianet Newsable
articles.summary: AMD’s Lisa Su Visits South Korea, Reportedly Discusses AI Collaboration With Samsung, SK Hynix  Asianet Newsable
articles.full_text:
AMD Chairperson and CEO Lisa Su met with senior leadership from Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix in South Korea to bolster supply chain ties and expand AMD’s artificial intelligence research footprint.
- Lisa Su reportedly met with SK Hynix CEO Kwak Noh-jung and Samsung Electronics DS Division chief Jun Young-hyun to expand high-bandwidth memory (HBM) and supply chain collaboration.
- Su engaged with 13 local South Korean AI startups to promote integration into AMD’s ROCm software platform, aimed at challenging Nvidia’s market dominance.
- AMD outlined plans to launch an AI Center of Excellence in South Korea, hiring hundreds of local researchers following a memorandum of understanding with the science ministry.
Advanced Micro Devices Inc. (AMD) CEO Lisa Su traveled to South Korea on Wednesday to reinforce semiconductor supply chain partnerships and broaden the company’s artificial intelligence hardware and software footprint in the region, according to South Korean news outlet The Chosun Daily.
The outreach comes as AMD intensifies competition with Nvidia Corp. (NVDA) in the rapidly growing market for AI accelerators, which rely heavily on advanced memory components and specialized software platforms.
AMD stock slipped about 0.6% on Wednesday.
Memory And Supply Chain Alliances
During her visit, Su met with key South Korean semiconductor leadership, including Kwak Noh-jung, chief executive of SK Hynix Inc., and Jun Young-hyun, head of Samsung Electronics Co.’s Device Solutions Division, The Chosun Daily reported.
The meetings centered on securing and expanding partnerships for high-bandwidth memory (HBM), an essential component used in AI accelerators to execute high-speed, large-scale computational tasks. Industry analysts also view Samsung as a viable potential partner for foundry chip manufacturing.
Speaking at a media briefing in Seoul, Su highlighted the critical role local suppliers play in the company’s global operations, saying Samsung and SK Hynix remain key partners on which AMD relies heavily.
Expanding The ROCm Software Ecosystem
In addition to discussions with major memory manufacturers, Su hosted a meeting with representatives from 13 South Korean AI startups and technology firms, including FuriosaAI, DeepX, Fadu, and Upstage.
The gathering focused on integrating local hardware and software developers into AMD’s open-source ROCm platform—an initiative designed to provide an alternative to Nvidia’s dominant CUDA software architecture.
Later in the day, Su attended the "AMD Gamer Day" event in Seoul's Yongsan District, reiterating the company's commitment to graphics processing unit (GPU) development alongside its enterprise AI push.
Investment In Local AI Research Hub
AMD is also moving forward with plans to bolster South Korea’s domestic technology sector. Following a memorandum of understanding signed with the Ministry of Science and ICT in July, Su detailed plans to establish an AMD AI Center of Excellence in the country.
The proposed research facility is expected to employ hundreds of AI researchers dedicated to advancing next-generation computing technologies and supporting the local tech ecosystem.
AMD Stock: Retail View
Retail sentiment on Stocktwits was ‘neutral’ with ‘normal’ message volumes.
AMD stock has gained about 205% year-to-date.

articles.title: N. Korea gains confidence as nuclear power 20 years after 1st test - Japan Wire by Kyodo News
articles.summary: N. Korea gains confidence as nuclear power 20 years after 1st test  Japan Wire by Kyodo News
articles.full_text:
BEIJING - North Korea has gained confidence as a nuclear power, having boosted its weapons stockpile and rejected denuclearization demands from the international community, as Friday marks 20 years since it conducted its first nuclear test.
In recent years, North Korea has deepened military cooperation with Russia as the two countries signed in 2024 a comprehensive strategic partnership treaty, which stipulates mutual support in times of emergency.
North Korea has also improved its ties with China, its largest trading partner and longtime economic benefactor, through mutual high-level visits. Chinese President Xi Jinping, during his first visit to North Korea in seven years in June, made no public mention of its nuclear program, which was seen as an apparent win for Pyongyang.
With North Korea becoming more politically and economically stable with the backing of the two neighbors, negotiating its denuclearization appears more difficult than ever.
Even U.S. President Donald Trump, who has shown eagerness to resume in-person talks with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, has publicly called the country a "nuclear power," despite Washington's official, long-standing policy of seeking its complete denuclearization.
Between 2006 and 2017, North Korea conducted a total of six nuclear tests. In a constitutional change in 2012, it proclaimed its status as a nuclear power.
The Stockholm International Peace Research Institute estimates North Korea has assembled around 60 nuclear warheads and possesses enough fissile material to make at least 30 more.
Negotiations on the denuclearization of the Korean Peninsula, involving the two Koreas, China, Japan, Russia and the United States, were held between 2003 and 2008, but effectively broke down amid disputes over verification methods.
During his first presidency, Trump met with Kim three times, with the initial Singapore summit in 2018 followed by meetings in 2019 in Vietnam and at the inter-Korean truce village of Panmunjeom.
But their denuclearization talks collapsed when the two leaders met in Hanoi, as they failed to bridge the gap between U.S. demands and North Korea's call for sanctions relief.
North Korea has long sought recognition as a nuclear-weapon state, demanding that status and the abandonment of the U.S. hostile policy toward it as preconditions for resuming bilateral talks.
With support from Russia and China -- both permanent members of the U.N. Security Council -- sanctions imposed over Pyongyang's nuclear and ballistic missile programs appear to be losing their effectiveness.
In 2024, Russia vetoed the renewal of a U.N. panel that was established in 2009 to monitor North Korea's adherence to international sanctions, leading to its disbandment. China abstained from the vote.
As part of its nuclear development, North Korea may have been conducting training to operate a small-scale reactor intended for installation aboard a nuclear-powered submarine under development, said Yuki Kobayashi, senior research fellow at the Sasakawa Peace Foundation in Tokyo who is well-versed in nuclear nonproliferation.
The training was believed to be held at a light-water reactor facility with an output capacity of 100,000 kilowatts in the Yongbyon nuclear complex in North Korea's northwest, according to the expert.
In 2023, the International Atomic Energy Agency said it had detected indicators of the reactor reaching "criticality," in which nuclear fuel sustains a fission chain reaction.
According to IAEA analysis, operations at the reactor were suspended between September and October in 2024, in April 2025, from August to November that year, and from March to April in 2026.
Due to the high frequency of the stoppages, speculation has grown among Japanese nuclear experts that they were part of light-water reactor startup drills conducted in preparation for operating a nuclear-powered submarine.

articles.title: NIS excluded from June meeting with US, Japan over N. Korean cyber threats - The Korea Times
articles.summary: NIS excluded from June meeting with US, Japan over N. Korean cyber threats  The Korea Times
articles.full_text:
The National Intelligence Service (NIS) was left out of a June trilateral meeting with Washington and Tokyo on North Korean cyber threats, the agency effectively acknowledged Thursday.
The exclusion belatedly came to light after a local newspaper reported that the spy agency had been barred from the fifth meeting of the Trilateral Diplomatic Working Group at the request of the U.S. side.
"There had been some misunderstanding several months ago, but it is now a thing of the past," the NIS said, all but acknowledging the report.
"Among states, misunderstandings can happen over different national interests. What matters is how to solve them in a timely manner," it said, adding, "There is no misunderstanding between intelligence authorities of South Korea and the U.S."
"The NIS is working closely with the U.S. side on security matters such as cyber and North Korea," it said.
The trilateral working group held its inaugural meeting in December 2023, following the summit between the leaders at Camp David, Maryland, in August that year, when they agreed to strengthen security cooperation.
The June session is believed to be the first without the NIS. The meeting brought together more than 60 participants from relevant ministries and agencies of the three countries to exchange assessments of North Korea's illicit cyber activities and discuss ways to effectively counter cyber threats.
The U.S. request is believed to have been prompted by Unification Minister Chung Dong-young's remarks during a parliamentary session in March that North Korea runs a third uranium enrichment facility in Kusong, alongside in Yongbyon and Kangson.
Chung has said he only shared what was already in the public domain.

articles.title: China border town can’t shake the blues despite promise of bridge to North Korea - The Straits Times
articles.summary: China border town can’t shake the blues despite promise of bridge to North Korea  The Straits Times
articles.full_text:
AI generated
DANDONG, Liaoning – Chinese taxi driver Wang peered through binoculars at a North Korean flag fluttering beyond a soon-to-open bridge linking his city of Dandong with the secretive nation.
“They finally finished their side,” said the 40-year-old, one of dozens who gathered this week near the New Yalu River Bridge in the north-eastern city, amid rumours that its opening will soon end a 12-year delay.
Coffee shops, a fun fair and a Little Yellow Duck theme park are springing up nearby, suggesting the struggling city hopes to cash in on the new link, but some residents and shopkeepers see it more as a curiosity than an economic boon.
“It won’t bring much new business here as regular citizens can’t visit, but they’re still our friends,” Wang told Reuters during a visit on Oct 6, the 77th anniversary of the neighbours’ diplomatic ties, referring to North Koreans.
While China completed the bridge in 2014, hoping to boost trade ties, North Korea left its approach roads and Customs facilities unfinished as relations soured over Pyongyang’s nuclear tests and the UN sanctions that followed.
Work resumed after a thaw in ties led to a June visit by Chinese President Xi Jinping, with both capitals having restored train services and direct flights, though neither has set a date to open the bridge.
The North Korean Customs house appeared complete, while green signs were lit up over the gate on the Chinese side, though no traffic crossed.

The opening of the new bridge would show progress in ties, within weeks of North Korea opening its first road bridge with Russia.
Faded border town
The bridge delay was a setback for Dandong, whose economy thrived in the early 21st century as the primary trade gateway to North Korea’s isolated economy.
For now, most goods still cross about 10km upstream at an 83-year-old bridge with a rail track and a single-lane road. That remains the busiest of about 15 crossing points along the roughly 1,350km border.
Recovering trade ties carried China’s exports to North Korea to a six-year high of US$2.3 billion (S$2.95 billion) in 2025, or an annual increase of 25%, though still well short of levels before the UN sanctions in 2017.
The uptick appears to have brought little benefit to Dandong, whose economy grew just 0.3% in the first half of 2026 against a national figure of 4.7%, with investment falling a third and new home sales down 28%, city data shows.
Although government offices in the city moved in 2011 to the Dandong New Zone near the new bridge, the area remains largely residential, with many apartments vacant.
Low pay is one reason why few workers stick around, said Wang, adding that factory jobs in the locality pay only about 3,000 yuan (S$570) a month.
‘Cut off from the world’
There is also little optimism for an economic revival at a trade zone in Dandong called Guomenwan that is just a five-minute drive from the Chinese side of the new bridge.
Launched in 2015 with a reported investment of 1 billion yuan, the complex now has mostly empty storefronts, with cafes, a vet clinic and a gym targeting the domestic market.
“This doesn’t have much to do with us,” a manager of the complex said when asked about the bridge’s opening, speaking on condition of anonymity.
In its first few years, the zone imported large volumes of North Korean seafood and farm products, he said. But subsequent UN Security Council resolutions banned such imports, as well as sales of steel and industrial machinery to Pyongyang.
“Business is slow here,” said Chen, a seller of curtains and fabric. “There aren’t that many people doing up their homes.”
Business is mostly local, added Chen, who gave only her surname, though she sometimes sees Chinese from ethnic Korean backgrounds working as middlemen, and the occasional North Korean buyer accompanied by an interpreter.
Yet, tourists still throng steadily to Dandong to gaze across the river, gathering at the old bridge where merchants sell snacks and offer enticements such as games of ring toss.
But there the journey stops. North Korea has not reopened to Chinese tourists since sealing its borders in 2020.
“They’ve cut themselves off from the world,” said Zhang, a passer-by at the new bridge. “It would be better to do more business with South Korea.” REUTERS

articles.title: Trade group crunches numbers on Trump’s impossible push for 100% US-made tech - Ars Technica
articles.summary: Trade group crunches numbers on Trump’s impossible push for 100% US-made tech  Ars Technica
articles.full_text:
One of Donald Trump’s biggest goals as president is to increase domestic manufacturing and reshore supply chains so that the most in-demand technologies in the world can be 100 percent made in the United States.
By executive order last December, he launched his “Genesis Mission,” an ambitious plan seeking to leverage US dominance in AI to maintain or seize an edge in advanced robotics, biotechnology, semiconductors, and nuclear technologies. According to Trump, that plan works best with self-sustaining supply chains. Not even neighboring countries or longtime allies should be relied upon to manufacture a single component of any US product in his ideal world.
The Consumer Technology Association (CTA) has long warned that Trump’s reshoring goals are not grounded in reality, but only recently has America’s largest technology trade association attempted to estimate what it would cost businesses and consumers to follow through on Trump’s plan.
“It is no longer enough to say that reshoring is difficult,” the CTA acknowledged. “The practical questions are what it would cost, product by product, what it would physically require, and who would pay for it.”
In new research shared with members this week, the CTA warned that reaching full US production of 10 categories of products most commonly found in US homes by 2031 “would require between $185 and $230 billion in capital expenditure, 555,000 to 668,000 additional full-time employees, and 19.1-19.5 billion kilowatt-hours of electricity per year.”
While the costs are eye-popping, the labor demand might be the bigger problem, requiring more than double the “existing US computer and electronics manufacturing workforce,” the CTA said. Additionally, the energy demand required to reshore all supply chains at once would clash with huge energy needs of AI data centers over the same time period.

articles.title: AMD Plans Tens of Billions in Asia as HBM4 Shortage Threatens AI Chip Growth - Coinpaper
articles.summary: AMD Plans Tens of Billions in Asia as HBM4 Shortage Threatens AI Chip Growth  Coinpaper
articles.full_text:
CEO Lisa Su said AMD is planning supply with partners three to five years ahead and encouraging memory producers to expand capacity as quickly as possible. During meetings in South Korea, she identified Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix as crucial suppliers while describing the memory environment as “very tight,” according to a report from Seoul Economic Daily.
The push builds on more than $10 billion AMD already committed to Taiwan earlier this year and comes as the company prepares to substantially increase AI-chip supply in 2027.
HBM4 Is Becoming a Bottleneck for AMD’s AI Expansion
AMD's next-generation Instinct MI455X accelerators and Helios rack-scale systems depend on HBM4, the latest generation of high-bandwidth memory designed to feed enormous amounts of data into AI processors.
Samsung signed an agreement in March to supply HBM4 for the MI455X, while AMD is also deepening cooperation with SK Hynix.
Su said the company is already shipping next-generation systems and wants both suppliers to increase production as AI data-center demand rises.
That matters because AMD's AI chip expansion is no longer limited by demand for its GPUs. The company increasingly needs enough memory, advanced wafers, packaging and server components to turn orders into deployed systems.
AMD Wants Much More Supply in 2027
Su said AMD has increased capacity this year but demand continues to exceed available supply.
The company therefore plans a substantial increase in 2027 production and is discussing additional wafer capacity with TSMC while exploring alternative advanced-packaging technologies.
AMD's earlier $10 billion Taiwan investment targets packaging and semiconductor infrastructure, but Su indicated spending across the wider supply chain could ultimately reach tens of billions.
The expansion follows extraordinary growth in AMD's Data Center business. Second-quarter revenue more than doubled year over year, helping push the company's market value above $1 trillion.
Investors have consequently begun treating AMD as a broader AI infrastructure platform rather than simply Nvidia's GPU challenger.
Samsung Could Become More Than a Memory Supplier
AMD is also considering deeper cooperation with Samsung beyond HBM.
Su confirmed the company continues to explore Samsung's foundry services, potentially giving AMD another manufacturing relationship alongside TSMC.
That diversification could become increasingly valuable if AI demand keeps stretching semiconductor capacity.
AMD's opportunity is enormous: its latest server CPU outlook points to growth across both GPUs and CPUs.

articles.title: Why Korea’s won stays weak despite export boom - Korea JoongAng Daily
articles.summary: Why Korea’s won stays weak despite export boom  Korea JoongAng Daily
articles.full_text:
Korea must curb liquidity to escape the triple-high trap
Despite record exports and a vast current account surplus, policy inconsistency, excess liquidity and semiconductor dependence are weighing on the won.
An employee sorts U.S. dollar bills at Hana Bank’s Anti-Counterfeiting Center in Jung District, central Seoul, on Oct. 6. According to the Bank of Korea, the country’s foreign exchange reserves stood at $440.56 billion at the end of September.YONHAP
Kim Jung-sik
The author is a professor emeritus of economics at Yonsei University and former president of the Korean Economic Association and the Korea International Economic Association.
GoogleAdmanager-KJD
One of the Korean economy’s biggest puzzles is why the won remains under depreciation pressure despite a substantial current account surplus and improving growth. Normally, these conditions should strengthen the currency.
Semiconductor demand pushed September exports to a record $120 billion, up 83.5 percent on year, putting annual exports of $1 trillion within reach. The Bank of Korea raised its growth forecast to 3.3 percent and projected a $450 billion current account surplus, approaching 20 percent of GDP.
Yet the exchange rate remains volatile. SK Hynix’s issuance of American depositary receipts increased dollar supply, temporarily strengthening the won to around 1,340 per dollar.
External factors include dollar strength, yen weakness, rising oil prices and increased Korean investment overseas. Expectations of annual $20 billion investments in the United States have also increased dollar demand. But these factors alone cannot explain the exchange rate’s behavior.
First, Korea depends excessively on semiconductor exports, particularly those driven by U.S. investment in AI. A U.S. downturn could severely damage Korean exports and the current account.
Meanwhile, Chinese competition has weakened other major industries, including automobiles and petrochemicals. Concerns about the sustainability of export growth are putting pressure on the won.
Second, contradictory monetary and fiscal policies are contributing to instability. Korea, the United States and Japan are combining monetary tightening to contain inflation with fiscal expansion to stimulate growth.
This combination can produce both high interest rates and excessive liquidity. Central banks seek to absorb liquidity through higher rates, while governments issue more bonds to finance spending.
Korea’s proposed budget increases spending by a record 12.8 percent. Government debt is projected to reach 1.7 quadrillion won ($1.27 trillion) by 2030. Even with stronger semiconductor-related tax revenues, fiscal expansion risks increasing inflation expectations and weakening the currency.
Large current account surpluses can also increase liquidity. During the late-1980s boom, characterized by low interest rates, exchange rates and oil prices, surpluses contributed to sharp increases in property and stock prices.
Although monetary authorities can absorb excess liquidity by issuing monetary stabilization bonds, substantial surpluses still inject money into the economy through multiple channels.
Third, inconsistent policies have undermined confidence. Frequent changes to real estate regulations and taxation, sometimes applied retroactively, discourage domestic investment and encourage capital outflows.
Expectations of won depreciation can also prompt investors to substitute dollars for domestic currency. The potential expansion of dollar-denominated stablecoins could intensify exchange rate volatility.
Addressing these vulnerabilities requires coordinated action.
The immediate priority should be reducing excess liquidity and inflation expectations. Housing regulations, lending restrictions and tax reforms cannot permanently stabilize property prices if abundant liquidity continues eroding money’s purchasing power.
The government must restrain excessive spending, while monetary authorities should manage liquidity generated by current account surpluses through effective interest rate policies.
Borrowing for living expenses stems from weak economic conditions and insufficient employment, while mortgage debt reflects elevated housing prices.
Simply tightening lending limits or raising interest rates cannot resolve these underlying problems. Instead, such measures risk increasing defaults and financial distress.
Financial regulators should prioritize reducing delinquency rates rather than restricting aggregate household lending. Stronger domestic demand, competitive industries, job creation and stable housing prices would help achieve a gradual reduction in household debt risks.
Central banks must also avoid abrupt rate increases that could trigger a debt crisis.
Restoring policy credibility is another priority. The government should avoid frequent regulatory changes and retroactive legislation. Predictable policies would encourage domestic investment and reduce demand for dollars as an alternative store of value.
Korea must also diversify its growth engines beyond semiconductors. Fiscal resources should prioritize research and development in emerging industries and training specialized workers rather than politically motivated spending.
New competitive industries could revive growth, attract domestic investment and stabilize the exchange rate.
Improving the business environment is equally essential. Labor regulations, taxation and investment rules should align with international standards.
In an economy with liberalized capital flows, uncompetitive regulations encourage money to leave the country through legal or illegal channels.
Rather than imposing capital controls, which carry substantial costs, policymakers should make domestic investment more attractive. Redirecting investment toward Korea would create jobs and support the won.
The exchange rate remains Korea’s economic Achilles’ heel. Heavy dependence on imported energy and raw materials means depreciation raises import prices, fuels inflation and encourages higher interest rates.
This creates the triple-high trap: high exchange rates, high inflation and high interest rates.
Although depreciation can benefit exporters, it can also undermine confidence, accelerate capital outflows and increase financial crisis risks.
The solution lies in credible policies, disciplined liquidity management and stronger industrial competitiveness. Without these measures, Korea risks remaining trapped in the triple-high economy.

articles.title: ‘Mirror’ Security Dilemma Fuels Sino-Japanese Tensions - orfonline.org
articles.summary: ‘Mirror’ Security Dilemma Fuels Sino-Japanese Tensions  orfonline.org
articles.full_text:
Japan and China increasingly view each other through interconnected theatres of strategic risk, creating a security dynamic in which each side’s response to insecurity reinforces the other’s perception of threat
The recently released 2026 Defence of Japan Pamphlet and Tsinghua University’s 2026 Overall Risk Landscape offer a revealing mirror image of how Japan and China increasingly view one another. Japan’s White Paper carries official endorsement, whereas the report by Tsinghua University’s Center for International Studies and Strategy (CISS) — which collates the views of many strategists — provides clues to how China appraises strategic risks.
The two assessments are strikingly reciprocal, though they do not assign each other identical strategic roles. Tokyo and Beijing appear caught in a mutually reinforcing security spiral. Japan increasingly reads China as the organising variable of its security environment, while China increasingly reads Japan not as an isolated regional rival but as a forward component of a wider US-led strategic architecture. Where Japan’s White Paper speaks of bolstering deterrence and response capabilities through bilateral and multilateral allies and partners, China perceives systematic containment. The result is a growing convergence in threat perception: each country sees the other as both an immediate security concern and an enabler of a larger, adverse strategic environment, and the two contest how developments in the Taiwan Strait, the East China Sea, and the wider Western Pacific are connected.
Where Japan’s White Paper speaks of bolstering deterrence and response capabilities through bilateral and multilateral allies and partners, China perceives systematic containment. The result is a growing convergence in threat perception: each country sees the other as both an immediate security concern and an enabler of a larger, adverse strategic environment.
The Japanese document describes China as an “unprecedented and the greatest strategic challenge” and links its military expansion to developments across the East China Sea, Taiwan, and the Western Pacific, as well as to China-Russia cooperation. What stands out in the Japanese assessment is the extent to which China has become the connective tissue of Tokyo’s security outlook. Taiwan, the East China Sea, the South China Sea, alliance management, defence-industrial policy, and even the transformation of Japan’s defence capabilities increasingly derive their urgency from Chinese military power. This is a significant shift from treating China as one among several regional contingencies. North Korea remains an acute and immediate threat, and Russia poses its own challenges, but China is presented as the actor whose expanding capabilities can affect multiple theatres simultaneously. The implication is that Japan no longer sees its security environment as compartmentalised: a contingency in one maritime space can quickly generate consequences in another.
Taiwan best illustrates this changing geography of Japanese threat perception. Tokyo’s concern is no longer confined to whether conflict might occur across the Strait, but increasingly extends to the operational consequences of a Taiwan contingency for Japan’s southwestern islands, sea lanes, and alliance commitments. The Japanese paper notes China’s intensified military activities around Taiwan, its efforts to create a fait accompli through PLA operations, and the possibility of a grey-zone blockade involving the China Coast Guard. Japan thus increasingly views Taiwan not simply as a distant political dispute but as a contingency that could transform the strategic environment immediately adjacent to Japanese territory.
This is precisely where the Tsinghua report offers a parallel image. Taiwan is identified as China’s foremost external security risk, but, in its framing, the danger stems from the convergence of political developments in Taiwan, US engagement, and Japan’s deepening involvement. More broadly, the report warns of an unprecedented “three-seas linkage” connecting the East China Sea, the Taiwan Strait, and the South China Sea. Japan’s perceived growing intent to intervene in Taiwan is therefore seen not as an isolated bilateral problem but as part of a wider effort to generate simultaneous pressure along China’s periphery. The strategic irony is clear: Japan sees Chinese pressure around Taiwan as bringing the threat closer to Japan, while China sees Japanese involvement in Taiwan as carrying the threat to its own doorstep.
The East China Sea is where these competing strategic maps overlap most directly. For Japan, Chinese activities around the Senkaku Islands are evidence of persistent attempts to alter the status quo through coercion. The Japanese paper places these activities within China’s broader expansion from the East China Sea into the Western Pacific. For Beijing, however, the East China Sea is increasingly inseparable from the Taiwan question. The Tsinghua report’s “three-seas” framework effectively treats the East China Sea as part of a connected maritime frontier rather than a separate sovereignty dispute. Meanwhile, the China Coast Guard’s presence around the Senkaku/Diaoyu Islands has become steadily more persistent: according to the chief of the China Coast Guard, Chinese vessels operated in the surrounding contiguous zone on 357 days in 2025.
Japan figures prominently in China’s security-risk calculus, with the bilateral relationship, perceived to be at its lowest ebb, having moved from “manageable friction” to “structural competition”. Tensions flared in November 2025 after Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s assertion that a Taiwan contingency involving the use of force could constitute a “survival-threatening situation” for Japan, one in which Tokyo could exercise the right of collective self-defence under its 2015 security legislation. Takaichi’s remark was prompted by a parliamentary question and did not form part of an official government statement. The Chinese government has described Taiwan as a “core interest”, underscoring its importance to China’s sovereignty and territorial integrity. Beijing holds the right-wing orientation of Takaichi’s administration responsible, accusing it of seeking to revive Japanese militarism. Chinese scholars such as Wu Jinan, a senior researcher at the Shanghai Institute for International Studies, have argued that Taiwan holds sentimental value in the “strategic calculations” of Japan’s conservatives, who regard it as part of their sphere of influence.
The Tsinghua report further foresees risks arising from an escalation of the dispute over the Diaoyu/Senkaku Islands and adjacent maritime spaces, deployments of US missiles, and the possibility of a conflagration following a collision involving aircraft or ships. Indeed, China has repeatedly conducted “law-enforcement patrolling” in the waters east of Taiwan since Japan and the Philippines announced that they intended to demarcate the maritime boundary between their exclusive economic zones (EEZs) and continental shelves. Beijing has asserted its right to patrol the area to protect the rights of Chinese fisherfolk and national sovereignty. It is in this context that the risk flagged in the Tsinghua report—the linkage of the three seas and the resulting interconnectedness of the maritime theatres—becomes tangible. What Tokyo and Manila see as a bilateral maritime delimitation, Beijing reads as a wider alignment between the two countries on the question of Taiwan’s sovereignty.
The Japanese White Paper observes that rivalry and competition between states have blurred the line between security and the economy, making it imperative to strengthen economic-security measures by building supply-chain resilience and safeguarding advanced technologies. The Tsinghua report similarly perceives an increasing entanglement of economics and security, and foresees further technology curbs that aim to systemically contain China. Yet it is China that has used supply chains as a lever: its Ministry of Commerce has restricted rare-earth exports to Japan, justifying the move as retaliation for Takaichi’s comments on Taiwan. Since Beijing itself treats supply chains as an instrument of leverage, the Tsinghua report in effect projects some of its own fears onto the future actions of other nations.
The deeper problem is that each country increasingly reads the other’s actions as demanding an immediate strategic response. Tokyo sees a China whose military, maritime, and grey-zone activities are steadily eroding the boundaries between separate contingencies. Beijing sees a Japan whose military transformation and posture on Taiwan are embedding it more deeply within a regional containment architecture. The danger lies in this reciprocal consolidation of threat perception. Once Taiwan and the East China Sea cease to be separate disputes and become mutually reinforcing theatres, pressure in one can be used to signal resolve in the other. Rivalry then turns self-referential: each side’s effort to manage its own insecurity becomes further evidence of hostile intent in the eyes of the other.
There are implications for New Delhi too. Against the backdrop of a protracted border standoff in recent years, the Tsinghua report mentions India in the context of the possibility of its using “terrorist organizations” against China. It also voices concern about the threat of terrorism to Beijing’s investments in the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC), which runs through territory under Pakistan’s occupation.
It is worth noting in this connection that the Chinese readout of the meeting between Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Chinese President Xi Jinping on the sidelines of the 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi quotes India as assuring China that there has been no change in its policies on Taiwan and Tibet, and that Indian territory would not be used for “anti-China” activities, even though the Indian reado

articles.title: AMD seeks 'broader partnership' with Samsung as it looks to secure memory supply — Samsung reportedly 'hopes to turn its memory supply relationship with AMD into foundry' orders for logic chips - Tom's Hardware
articles.summary: AMD seeks 'broader partnership' with Samsung as it looks to secure memory supply — Samsung reportedly 'hopes to turn its memory supply relationship with AMD into foundry' orders for logic chips  Tom's Hardware
articles.full_text:
A little less than seven months since signing a memorandum of understanding (MOU) concerning memory supply and collaboration in various fields with Samsung, AMD's chief executive Lisa Su is visiting South Korea to secure additional supply of HBM memory for AI accelerators, reports Chosun.biz. Meanwhile, Samsung is seeking a broader partnership and 'hopes to turn its memory supply relationship with AMD into foundry' chip production orders, the report claims.
"We are going to talk about our broader partnership," said Lisa Su when asked by reporters about what she planned to discuss with Samsung's executives. "We have many partners at Samsung."
Before visiting Samsung headquarters, Lisa Su and Jack Huynh, senior vice president and general manager of AMD's Computing and Graphics Group, attended the AMD Gamer Day event where Su and Huynh answered some questions from South Korean journalists and called local memory makers 'important strategic partners,' something that reflects the significance of data center-grade DDR5 and HBM memory for the company's AI and data center businesses.
"Samsung Electronics and SK hynix are key supply-chain partners for AMD," Su said, Chosun reports. "AI demand is extremely high, so we are planning our long-term supply chain with our partners. […] It is important to plan three to five years ahead with our partners."
The non-binding MOU that AMD and Samsung signed this March covered four areas and remained in effect for a period of three years:
- Supply of next-generation memory products, including HBM4 and advanced DDR5;
- Co-development and optimization of memory solutions for Al and high-performance computing systems;
- Exploration of foundry manufacturing opportunities for the future AMD platforms;
- Co-optimization of advanced packaging and related semiconductor technologies.
While Samsung has become a principal supplier of HBM4 for AMD's Instinct MI400-series accelerators, expansion of collaboration beyond memory supply is considerably more complicated, as it involves considerable efforts to design chips for Samsung Foundry's process technologies as well as risks associated with a product ramp at a new contract chipmaker. Truth to be told, AMD already uses Samsung Foundry and UMC to make its "ICs in the form of programmable logic devices" however, moving production of more advanced products to Samsung is risky. Meanwhile, Samsung badly needs big customers like AMD, and the latter's dependence on HBM supply certainly gives the former leverage.
"If we transition the production of some of our products to new manufacturers, we may experience delayed product introductions, lower yields or poorer performance of our products," AMD wrote in its most recent Annual Report.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
AMD has already started shipments of its Instinct MI455 accelerators with 432GB of HBM4 memory onboard as well as rack-scale Helios AI systems to interested parties.
"We have started shipping our next-generation MI455 and Helios systems," Su told journalists, according to Chosun. "These are all systems that use HBM4."
So, it looks like the company is negotiating for more memory supply. The question is, will it take a risk and adopt Samsung Foundry for something more serious than niche programmable chips in a bid to get more high-bandwidth memory and sell more expensive AI accelerators? Only time will tell.

Anton Shilov is a contributing writer at Tom’s Hardware. Over the past couple of decades, he has covered everything from CPUs and GPUs to supercomputers and from modern process technologies and latest fab tools to high-tech industry trends.

articles.title: Spanish politicians trade blame after death of octogenarian at heart of housing protests - The Standard (HK)
articles.summary: Spanish politicians trade blame after death of octogenarian at heart of housing protests  The Standard (HK)
articles.full_text:
Spanish politicians traded blame on Thursday after the death of an 87-year-old woman who was evicted from her Madrid home exacerbated heated debates over housing ahead of an early election next month, as protests raged on across the country.
Maricarmen Abascal, who died on Wednesday, had been hospitalised for severe anxiety and exhaustion since her dramatic eviction on September 23, though no cause of death has been announced.
News that she had died enraged protesters camped out on squares in Spain's main cities, who chanted that she had been "murdered" by the greed of her landlords.
"When everything is private, we will be deprived of everything," said one placard on Madrid's Puerta del Sol square where mourners lit candles and left flowers honouring Maricarmen, as she has become known across Spain.
Protests over housing shortages and surging rents sparked by Maricarmen's eviction prompted Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez to call a snap general election on November 29. Following her death, political leaders were quick to invoke Maricarmen in their attacks on opponents.
Left-leaning parties criticised the conservatives who had shot down decrees with housing measures aiming to curb soaring rental prices, while right-wingers said the leftist central government had proven unable to tackle the crisis after eight years in power.
In the capital, Madrid, lawmakers accused each other of cynically exploiting Abascal's case.
The conservative People's Party (PP), which has absolute majorities in the Madrid regional and local assemblies, refused to hold a minute of silence honouring Maricarmen, prompting hard-left deputies to stage one outside City Hall.
They also gave her a 60-second standing ovation during a tense debate in the regional assembly, while PP lawmakers remained seated with folded arms.
Madrid leader Isabel Diaz Ayuso of the PP blamed Sanchez, pointing out that the eviction had occurred under his government.
Opposition leader Manuela Bergerot of the leftist Mas Madrid party said Maricarmen had died because of "miserable people who put gain above a person's life ... those responsible will carry that with them for their remaining days."
She added that the last thing Ayuso had done while Maricarmen was alive was "laugh at her" — a reference to when Ayuso quipped on September 28: "At what age do I get to stop paying my landlords? Let me know."
(Reuters)

articles.title: Samsung Eyes $80 Billion Profit as AI Demand Drives Chip Sales - PhoneWorld
articles.summary: Samsung Eyes $80 Billion Profit as AI Demand Drives Chip Sales  PhoneWorld
articles.full_text:
Samsung Electronics expects a major jump in quarterly profit as demand for artificial intelligence (AI) technology continues to boost the global semiconductor industry.
The South Korean technology giant estimates that its operating profit for the three months ending in September will reach 107.4 trillion won ($80 billion). This would represent a roughly nine-fold increase from the same period last year and mark Samsung’s fourth consecutive quarter of record earnings.
The company will release its complete third-quarter financial results at the end of October. However, Samsung has issued an early earnings forecast to give investors an indication of its expected performance.
Samsung Eyes $80 Billion Profit as AI Demand Drives Chip Sales
The strong results are largely linked to rising demand for memory chips used in AI data centres. AI companies require large quantities of high-performance memory and other advanced semiconductors to train and operate increasingly powerful AI systems.
Samsung is one of the world’s largest memory chip manufacturers. It is competing with SK Hynix of South Korea and Micron of the United States. Their chips are used in AI infrastructure developed by major technology companies, including Nvidia and other data-centre operators.
The rapid expansion of AI services has created strong demand for semiconductors and helped improve prices and sales across the industry.
Samsung Gets Support From Smartphone Business
Samsung’s semiconductor division is not the only part of the company expected to benefit. Its smartphone business could also receive a boost from the company’s latest foldable devices, which were launched in August.
Samsung remains one of the world’s largest smartphone manufacturers, with products including the Galaxy S26 series and Galaxy Fold lineup. Strong demand for its latest premium devices could provide additional support to its overall earnings.
However, the company’s expected profit surge is primarily being attributed to the semiconductor business and the ongoing AI-driven chip boom.
Global Investment in AI Chips Continues
The growing demand for AI computing has triggered a major increase in investment across the semiconductor and data-centre industries.
Major US technology companies, including Google, Amazon and Meta, will invest more than $650 billion in AI projects this year. Much of this spending is helping drive demand for computing infrastructure, processors and memory chips.
South Korea is also seeking to strengthen its position in the global semiconductor industry. In June, the country announced plans involving at least $880 billion in projects led by Samsung and SK Hynix to expand chip manufacturing capabilities over the coming years.
Companies in Japan, China and Taiwan are also investing heavily in new semiconductor facilities as they look to benefit from the long-term growth of AI.
See Also: Samsung Begins Mass Production of Exynos 2700 Ahead of Galaxy S27 Launch
Chip Shortage Pushes Up Prices
The rapid increase in demand for semiconductors has also created supply pressures in parts of the market. Manufacturers have responded by increasing chip prices as demand continues to outpace available supply for certain products.
Higher semiconductor costs can eventually affect consumer products, including smartphones and computers, potentially making some devices more expensive.
Samsung’s expected record earnings highlight how strongly the AI boom is affecting the wider technology industry. As companies continue to expand AI data centres and invest in advanced computing, demand for memory chips is expected to remain an important source of growth for major semiconductor manufacturers.

articles.title: Samsungs Operating Profit Jumps Nearly Ninefold To Record $80.1 Billion, Misses Estimates Amid AI Chip Boom - Free Press Journal
articles.summary: Samsungs Operating Profit Jumps Nearly Ninefold To Record $80.1 Billion, Misses Estimates Amid AI Chip Boom  Free Press Journal
articles.full_text:
Samsung Electronics reported a nearly ninefold increase in quarterly operating profit, supported by soaring demand for memory chips used in artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure. However, the record earnings fell short of market expectations.
According to a report by Bloomberg, the South Korean technology giant posted preliminary operating profit of 107.4 trillion won ($80.1 billion) for the quarter ended September, while revenue reached 195 trillion won.
Both figures were below analysts' estimates, reflecting the exceptionally high expectations surrounding the global AI investment boom.
Samsung shares remained largely unchanged during early trading in Seoul on Thursday.
AI chip demand drives Samsung's record profit
The rapid expansion of AI infrastructure has increased demand for advanced memory products, particularly high-bandwidth memory (HBM) used alongside Nvidia processors and other AI accelerators.
Demand for flash memory and low-power chips has also strengthened, benefiting major manufacturers including Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron Technology.
Counterpoint Research increased its forecast for third-quarter dynamic random-access memory (DRAM) prices to a sequential rise of 10% to 20%, compared with its earlier estimate of 5% to 10%.
The research firm attributed the revision partly to customers advancing their orders.
Samsung faces investor caution despite semiconductor boom
The AI spending surge has transformed Samsung's semiconductor operations following an earlier industry downturn that resulted in substantial losses.
The recovery has also strengthened South Korea's exports, with semiconductor shipments more than tripling year-on-year in September.
Analysts expect Samsung's chip division to report operating profit of 110 trillion won, while its electronics business is projected to record a loss.
The company will publish its detailed financial results on Oct 29.
Despite record earnings announced in July, Samsung shares remain approximately 25% below their June peak.
Investors remain cautious about the semiconductor industry's historically cyclical performance.
Meanwhile, Samsung and SK Hynix are expanding manufacturing capacity and increasing investments in AI companies to support future demand.

articles.title: SK Hynix to Cut Semiconductor Environmental Footprint with AI — Establishes 'AI Environmental Research Institute' - BigGo Finance
articles.summary: SK Hynix to Cut Semiconductor Environmental Footprint with AI — Establishes 'AI Environmental Research Institute'  BigGo Finance
articles.full_text:
SK Hynix is creating a dedicated research organization to leverage artificial intelligence (AI) technology in reducing the environmental burden generated during semiconductor production. The company formalized its plan to establish an "AI Environmental Research Institute" on the 8th at the "Public-Private Joint K-GX (Korean-style Green Transformation) Strategy Declaration Ceremony" held at the Korea Chamber of Commerce and Industry in Seoul.
The new institute will focus on improving energy supply efficiency for semiconductor fabs and data center operations, and on developing technologies that lower environmental loads across the entire manufacturing process. Key priorities include AI algorithm-based power demand forecasting, maximizing data center cooling efficiency, developing alternative gases to reduce greenhouse gas emissions from semiconductor manufacturing, and advancing process water purification and recycling technologies.
The research scope also includes developing biodegradable eco-friendly semiconductor materials and e-waste resource circulation technologies. The company's vision is to apply AI to environmental and geographical challenges that are difficult to solve with existing technologies alone. In the research agenda-setting process, SK Hynix plans to gather input from government, academia, civic groups, and local communities, and to pursue science-based regional environmental improvement initiatives.
A "Decarbonization Transition Center" will be established as a separate unit within the institute. The dedicated team will provide customized consulting and support on greenhouse gas reduction, energy savings, and low-carbon process adoption to approximately 1,700 South Korean semiconductor equipment, parts, and materials suppliers that do business with SK Hynix.
The goal is to elevate the response capabilities of the entire South Korean semiconductor supply chain — not just SK Hynix alone — amid a landscape where global information technology (IT) companies are demanding supply chain-level carbon reductions and countries are tightening environmental regulations.
Chey Tae-won, chairman of the Korea Chamber of Commerce and Industry, attended the previous day's event in his capacity as head of the private-sector consultative body, stating, "We must create a virtuous cycle where AI technology accelerates the pace of green transformation, and green transformation in turn supports the sustainable growth of the AI industry." He added, "SK Hynix will also align with this vision by establishing the AI Environmental Research Institute and taking the lead in the eco-friendly transformation of the semiconductor ecosystem."
Kim Hyung-hwan, head of safety, health, and environment at SK Hynix, emphasized, "Through the AI Environmental Research Institute, we will wisely solve the complex environmental challenges facing the semiconductor industry," adding, "In particular, we will enhance the carbon competitiveness of the entire semiconductor ecosystem, with the Decarbonization Transition Center at the core."
Environmental Challenges Triggered by Surging AI Semiconductor Demand
The institute's establishment comes in response to the power and water consumption and carbon emissions accompanying the rapid growth of AI semiconductor production. Manufacturing AI chips requires significantly more energy and ultrapure water than conventional general-purpose semiconductors, and data center operations also demand enormous amounts of electricity.
SK Hynix holds a leading position in the AI memory semiconductor market, including high-bandwidth memory (HBM), which means its environmental footprint expands as production volumes grow. The company's decision to use AI technology itself to address environmental problems is seen as an attempt to resolve this paradox through technology.
Applying AI to power demand forecasting can optimize energy use at fabs and data centers, while cooling efficiency improvements can simultaneously reduce both costs and carbon emissions in the cooling segment, which accounts for a substantial portion of data center power consumption.
Carbon Pressure Extending Across the Supply Chain
The establishment of the Decarbonization Transition Center is driven by tightening global supply chain regulations. With the European Union's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) and supply chain due diligence directives now in full effect, carbon emissions data management and low-carbon transition have become essential tasks not only for large corporations but also for their suppliers.
SK Hynix's move to provide customized consulting and support to approximately 1,700 suppliers is also a measure to reduce the "Scope 3" emissions of its products — the indirect emissions generated across the entire supply chain. The growing number of global IT companies demanding supply chain carbon information disclosure in semiconductor procurement has also been a contributing factor.
Industry observers note that the institute could serve as a catalyst for elevating the environmental response capabilities of South Korea's semiconductor ecosystem to the next level. However, some point out that since research outcomes may take considerable time to be applied to actual manufacturing processes, the specificity of the mid- to long-term roadmap matters more than short-term results.

articles.title: Trump complained about the weak yen. Days later, Japan PM Takaichi signals the end of reflation - The Straits Times
articles.summary: Trump complained about the weak yen. Days later, Japan PM Takaichi signals the end of reflation  The Straits Times
articles.full_text:
While Takaichi promises a ‘responsible, proactive fiscal policy’, analysts warn that her statements are mere messaging that masks deep structural flaws.
AI generated
TOKYO – Ever since US President Donald Trump voiced frustration over the weak yen during a late September summit with Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, Japan has moved quickly to declare that its era of reflation is over.
Delivering her parliamentary policy speech on Oct 5, Takaichi described 2026 as the “first year of responsible, proactive fiscal policy”.
On Oct 8, she rejected the “reflationary” label at a parliamentary debate, saying: “We are promoting domestic investment to raise Japan’s potential growth rate, increase quality employment and incomes, improve consumer sentiment, boost corporate earnings and ultimately lead to a natural tax-revenue increase.”
Notwithstanding Takaichi’s expansive policy programmes, her underlying message was unmistakable: Gone is the era of “Abenomics”, the signature policy package championed by her late political mentor and former prime minister Shinzo Abe.
Reflationary economics, as symbolised by Abenomics in Japan, uses government and central bank policies to stimulate economic activity to reverse a deflation or downturn.
For over a decade, Abenomics attempted to shock Japan out of its long deflationary slumber through reflation by pumping money into the economy through low interest rates, heavy government spending, and central bank money printing.
Analysts who spoke to The Straits Times, however, believe Takaichi’s move was calculated political signalling aimed at appeasing Washington and calming volatile financial markets – without a clear change in substance.

Lawyer Lim Tean handed 3 more charges including committing act that could defeat course of justice

Business
OpenAI’s Singapore-based APAC policy head leaving job after 6 months, source says
The “reflation is over” messaging followed a tense exchange with Trump in New York on Sept 22.
In an interview with Nippon TV on Oct 1, Takaichi acknowledged that Trump had complained that American exporters were suffering due to the cheap yen, prompting her to concede that the currency’s undervaluation was indeed a problem.
Yet behind closed doors, her reaction was reportedly far sharper. The Nikkei newspaper quoted Takaichi venting to her aides after the meeting: “Why does Japan have to listen to the US’ concerns?”
The immediate pressure stems from a growing global interest rate gap. As major central banks raised interest rates to fight inflation, Japan kept its borrowing costs low. Global investors dumped the yen to seek higher returns elsewhere, driving its value down by over 50 per cent against the US dollar since 2020 to hover near 40-year lows of around 164 per dollar in July.
A weak yen is cheered by foreign tourists and inflates the foreign earnings of Japanese exporters, but it undercuts US manufacturers as Japanese alternatives become cheaper worldwide. At home, it hurts households by driving up import costs for daily groceries and fuel. In Tokyo, core consumer inflation rose to 2.7 per cent year-on-year in September.
Managing bilateral trade friction while relying on Washington as its sole security partner is a familiar dance for Tokyo.
“Washington has considerable political leverage, particularly when exchange rates become linked to trade negotiations and the broader bilateral relationship,” former Bank of Japan (BOJ) board member Sayuri Shirai, now a professor at Keio University, told ST.
“US pressure makes it harder for Tokyo to appear comfortable with persistent yen weakness,” she said. “The risk of friction would increase if Washington concluded that Japan was deliberately pursuing policies that perpetuate an undervalued yen.”
Stefan Angrick, head of Asia-Pacific economics at Moody’s Analytics, told ST that he believed the debate was “mostly about messaging rather than economic substance”.
“To the extent that Japan now has inflation, conditions are clearly different from the deflationary decades before the pandemic. Moving away from the language of reflation is, therefore, sensible and probably politically expedient,” he said.
“Even advocates of more proactive fiscal policy would agree that the government doesn’t want to create the impression that ‘anything goes’,” he added.
Historically, Washington has not hesitated to use its trade leverage against Tokyo, from the 1970s trade disputes and the 1985 Plaza Accord – which forced a massive yen appreciation – to the 1989 Structural Impediments Initiative targeting Japanese market entry barriers.
More recent US administrations have pushed Tokyo to buy more American automobiles and agricultural products. And Trump’s threats of imposing “reciprocal” tariffs resulted in Japan, already the largest foreign direct investor in America, pledging US$550 billion (S$705 billion) in strategic US investments.
‘Stop the reflation’
Now, with the cheap yen frustrating US exporters and unsettling the US Treasury market, where Japan is the largest foreign holder of American government debt, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has bluntly warned Tokyo to “stop the reflation”.
To prop up the tumbling currency, Japanese authorities have poured more than 27 trillion yen (S$219 billion) into market interventions in 2026 alone.
In July, Washington and Tokyo even executed a rare joint intervention, stepping into foreign exchange markets together to buy yen for the first time since the 1998 Asian financial crisis, though the currency gains proved short-lived.
Compounding the problem, financial markets remain deeply nervous over Japan’s underlying fiscal health. Gross public debt sits at about 200 per cent of GDP, the highest in the developed world.
Takaichi, widely regarded as a fiscal dove who favours heavy spending over budget restraint, is perceived to have been wary of the BOJ raising interest rates, given that higher borrowing costs could derail her economic agenda.
On Oct 1, the release of a summary of opinions from the BOJ’s mid-September meeting – when the benchmark interest rate was raised to 1.25 per cent, its highest level in 31 years – revealed that a Cabinet Office representative had warned central bankers to “examine carefully the cumulative effects of past policy rate hikes”.
Markets interpreted this remark as political pressure against further interest rate hikes, sparking another round of yen selling.
Four days later in Parliament, Takaichi sought to reassure investors by emphasising her commitment to “responsible, proactive fiscal policy”. But she did not provide clear details even as she told markets “not to worry” about how her administration would cover an estimated 10 trillion yen tax revenue loss resulting from a planned two-year cut to the food consumption tax.
She also announced that her government will finalise a Growth Strategy Implementation Plan by year-end, which will spell out strategic priorities across 17 growth sectors, including artificial intelligence (AI), semiconductors, and shipbuilding. This builds on a broader commitment to mobilise 370 trillion yen in combined public and private investment by 2040.
More than slogans
This was not enough to convince veteran economist Richard Katz, who was dismissive of Takaichi’s growth plans as an “economic fantasy” built on weak foundations.
“There’s this myth that technology and investment automatically create growth. It’s not true,” Katz said.
“What creates growth are smart companies that know how to use investment and technology to turn them into economic value... The real underlying reason why the yen is so weak is because Japanese industry has become less competitive on the global stage.”
Keio University’s Shirai said that Takaichi must tackle structural weaknesses rather than rely on policy slogans.
“The key question is what replaces the earlier emphasis on monetary easing and fiscal expansion,” Shirai noted, adding that Tokyo must deliver “concrete measures that improve productivity, business investment, and household purchasing power.”
This requires clear strategies to alleviate severe labour shortages, accelerate digital transformation, and ensure AI investments translate into broad-based productivity gains across businesses.
“Large spending commitments do not automatically generate stronger growth or enough additional tax revenue to pay for themselves,” Shirai warned. “Japan needs to prioritise projects with demonstrable economic benefits.”
Only if Takaichi can demonstrate that her policies generate sustained growth and real income gains will Japan win lasting confidence in financial markets.
“That is ultimately a more meaningful test than whether the government calls its policies ‘reflationary’ or ‘responsible’,” Shirai said.

articles.title: Commerce Department Turns Chip Warning Letters Into Hard Law Before Truce Expires - Startup Fortune
articles.summary: Commerce Department Turns Chip Warning Letters Into Hard Law Before Truce Expires  Startup Fortune
articles.full_text:
Washington is converting a year of one-off warning letters to chipmakers into binding regulation, timed to land weeks before the US-China truce that has kept the chip war on pause expires.
The Commerce Department is rolling out a package of rules this week that takes restrictions it had previously handed down company by company, in private letters, and writes them into the Export Administration Regulations for everyone. The move formalizes limits on selling chipmaking tools capable of producing logic chips at 14 nanometers or finer, and tightens the licensing path for advanced AI and supercomputing chips bound for China. It lands just over a month before the one-year truce struck at the October 2025 APEC summit in Gyeongju, South Korea, runs out on November 9.
You don't normally see a government spend a year enforcing a policy through private correspondence and then turn around and codify it. But that's roughly what happened here. In April, Commerce sent individual letters to KLA, Lam Research and Applied Materials ordering them to stop shipping certain tools to Hua Hong, China's second-largest chip foundry, and its Huali Microelectronics subsidiary. The targets were specific: Hua Hong's Fab 6 in Shanghai, which runs 28 and 22 nanometer lines, and a second site, Fab 8a, that doesn't even appear on the company's own website. US officials suspected Huali was pushing toward a 7 nanometer process there, with Huawei reportedly lined up to shift some of its AI chip production to the site once it's running. Those letters applied to three companies. This week's rule applies to every equipment maker that sells into China, whether Commerce ever wrote them a letter or not.
The same pattern played out with chips themselves. Nvidia and AMD received letters earlier this year instructing them to stop shipping certain AI computing chips to China without a license. Codifying that guidance turns a warning aimed at two companies into a standing requirement for the whole industry, and it expands the foreign direct product rule, the mechanism that lets Washington reach foreign-made chips and tools if they contain enough US technology, to catch more Chinese entities than before.
The timing only makes sense against the truce it precedes. At the Gyeongju summit, the US agreed to suspend its "50% Rule," which would have extended export blacklisting to any company at least half-owned by an entity already on the list, for one year starting November 10, 2025. China, in turn, deferred its own export controls on rare earths and critical minerals, including gallium, germanium, antimony and graphite, items where it controls somewhere between 60% and 90% of global supply depending on the material. Both sides agreed to pause, not settle, their underlying fight. Now that pause is close to running out, and each government is visibly getting its instruments back in order before it does.
The Commerce Department has clarified that advanced AI chip export licenses apply to China-headquartered companies even when their overseas subsidiaries are the buyers. The move tightens a loophole around Nvidia’s Blackwell and Rubin systems and puts more compliance pressure on AI data center projects outside China. - how to buy Nvidia chips as foreign company - US export controls on advanced AI semiconductor sales
Here's the part that doesn't add up cleanly, though. This same administration spent much of 2026 easing the very restrictions it's now locking into law. It approved Nvidia's H200 chip for export to China on the condition that the US government collect 25% of the proceeds, a structure former officials criticized at the time as trading away a national security tool for revenue. It suspended the 50% Rule as part of the truce. Codifying the equipment and chip letters now reads less like a sudden crackdown and more like Washington hedging its bets: keep the door open for trade talks, but have the stricter rulebook ready to go the moment November 9 passes without a deal.
Nvidia, meanwhile, is dealing with a problem no license requirement has solved. The Financial Times reported that more than $1 billion worth of its AI chips, including B200, H100 and H200 models, were smuggled into China in the three months after the administration tightened export controls this year. Resellers in Guangdong, Zhejiang and Anhui provinces are reportedly selling the banned processors openly to AI data centers, and a repair industry has sprung up in Shenzhen that reportedly services as many as 500 of the chips a month. Some buyers are said to be sourcing hardware through Southeast Asian markets, including Thailand, rather than bringing chips into China directly. None of that activity touches the equipment rule Commerce is finalizing this week, which targets the machines that make chips, not the chips themselves, but it's the backdrop against which lawmakers are now scrutinizing whether Nvidia's chips are ending up in Chinese hands by design or by leakage.
Frankly, the chip war was never going to be settled by a one-year truce, and nobody in Washington seems to think it was. What this week's rule actually does is remove the ambiguity of letters that applied to three or four companies and replace it with something every equipment maker and chip designer has to plan around, truce or no truce. For KLA, Lam Research and Applied Materials, that means China revenue that was already uncertain just got a formal ceiling. For Nvidia, it means the license regime tightens on paper at the exact moment its chips are reportedly moving around it in practice.
